short: A sprawling retreat at Tivoli where Hadrian recreated buildings he admired from across the empire.
full:
Hadrian began building his villa near Tivoli, east of Rome, around 118 CE, soon after becoming emperor, and continued adding to it in phases until his death in 138. Rather than a single palace, it grew into an extensive landscape of more than thirty structures spread across roughly 120 hectares: bath complexes, a maritime theatre on its own moated island, libraries, a stadium-garden and a long canal, the Canopus, flanked by copies of Greek and Egyptian statuary and named for a city on the Nile that Hadrian had visited.

The villa functioned as a working seat of government as much as a retreat; Hadrian received envoys and conducted state business there in his later years, particularly after 128 CE when it became his primary residence. Its architecture experimented freely with curved walls, domed pavilions and unusual geometries that broke from standard Roman practice, likely reflecting Hadrian's own interests as a designer. Much of the site was stripped of statuary and marble by later collectors, including Renaissance popes, before systematic excavation began in the eighteenth century.
